transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-04
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen, Leo Park (Redwood); Dr. Priya Singh, Adrian Morales, Sophie Chen, Tomás Ruiz (Cygnus)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, optional):
- Quick console tour focused on org/project key patterns and fairburst allocation.
- Discussed hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, VPC/private deployment constraints, and SOC2/KMS concerns.
- Agreed to run a 2-week POC with benchmark script; Redwood to share pricing and security docs.

Topics:
- Org vs Project key topology
- Fairburst and quota shaping
- Console route policies + sticky routing
- Dedicated capacity pricing and SLAs
- Security (SOC2, KMS, audit logs, VPC)

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: All right everybody, thanks for joining — quick intro, this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, I have Leo who'll do the deep end of the demo, and Rina from product just listening in.
[00:08] Dr. Priya Singh: Hi, thanks. We are Priya, head of ML at Cygnus, we run a bunch of genomics inference pipelines, so throughput matters a lot.
[00:14] Adrian Morales: Adrian here, platform eng, curious about isolation and routing — we have multi-tenant workloads internally.
[00:20] Sophie Chen: Sophie from security, I'll be focusing on compliance questions, SOC2 and key management.
[00:27] Maya Chen: Great. Goal for today: show console flows for org/project keys, how fairburst and quota slicing works, and talk through a POC plan that gets you some real numbers. Is that aligned?
[00:35] Dr. Priya Singh: Yep, yep, perfect. Also would like to see cost estimates for our mix of short chat-ish requests and some long-batch token generation.
[00:42] Leo Park: Cool, I'll start with a short architecture diagram — please excuse the screen share lag — so this is Redwood's control plane, you can pin model variants, create orgs, then projects under orgs which map to API keys. Projects are where we attach quotas and sticky routing.
[00:58] [screen share started]
[01:12] Leo Park: Example topology: one org for Cygnus, projects per team, and you can have service keys for internal systems. We also support org-level quotas for global caps.
[01:25] Tomás Ruiz: When you say sticky routing, is that per-session or per-key? We have sessions for long-running batch jobs.
[01:30] Leo Park: Good question. Sticky routing can be set to sticky-per-key or sticky-per-session depending on the token you pass. For batch jobs we recommend per-session affinity so KV caches stay warm on the same GPU pool.
[01:45] Adrian Morales: How does this affect cost? If we pin sessions to GPU nodes, do we lose bin-packing efficiency?
[01:50] Rina Kapoor: There is a tradeoff — affinity reduces latency and warms the KV cache, which lowers per-token compute, but it can increase utilization fragmentation. Our console Optimize tab gives quantification — you can see estimated unit cost delta for affinity on/off.
[02:05] [00:02:05] Sophie Chen: On security: If we do dedicated, are logs and telemetry kept in the customer VPC?
[02:11] Maya Chen: For Private deployments yes, audit logs and traces can be routed to your S3/GCS or your SIEM in your VPC. For Dedicated (hosted dedicated pools) logs remain in Redwood control plane but we provide live-export hooks to your endpoint or SOC2 log bundle exports.
[02:26] Sophie Chen: And KMS? We need CMKs in our HSM.
[02:29] Leo Park: We integrate with KMS/HSM providers, you can bring your own CMKs via a supported integration. There's a slightly different flow for on-prem vs hosted.
[02:38] Dr. Priya Singh: Walk us through a typical quota config for a mixed workload: bursty API for developer tools and scheduled heavy batch runs for model scoring.
[02:45] Leo Park: Sure — couple approaches. Option A (org-level fairburst): create an org cap to limit total tokens/min, then per-project burst lanes that allow short high-rate bursts. Option B (project-based strict quotas): allocate monthly token budgets per project plus concurrency limits. We usually recommend hybrid: org cap for global backpressure plus project burst lanes for dev/test.
[03:05] [00:03:05] Adrian Morales: Hybrid sounds good. How do you handle backpressure when org cap is hit? Request routing fallback?
[03:11] Leo Park: We have automated fallback policies — you can route to a cheaper model variant, to a queued bucket, or return 429 with a retry-after. Console also supports priority lanes so important traffic (billing, core scoring) can bypass some caps.
[03:26] Dr. Priya Singh: Can we define priority lanes based on header metadata? e.g., X-Cygnus-Pipeline:core
[03:31] Leo Park: Yes, routing policies allow header-based matchers, JWT claim attributes, or source IP. They map to route rules.
[03:39] Maya Chen: Quick live demo: I'll create a project key, attach a burst window of 30 seconds with 2000 token allowance, and a monthly budget of 10M tokens, then show what happens when we send a synthetic traffic spike.
[03:52] [screen interaction noises — clicking]
[04:10] Maya Chen: Key created. Note: naming conventions are important — customers often do org.production.pipelineA to make it easy in logs.
[04:22] [04:22] Tomás Ruiz: That naming is helpful for our ingest pipelines. Can we rotate keys programmatically?
[04:27] Leo Park: Yes, we have a rotation API and SDK calls. You can also set automatic rotation interval in console.
[04:34] [04:34] Sophie Chen: About audit logs — do you keep the full request payload in logs? We need to avoid PII or sensitive genomic markers leaving our environment.
[04:44] Maya Chen: By default we redact request bodies in hosted mode; for Private deployments you control what gets exported. We also have configurable PII scrubbing and a retention policy.
[04:54] Dr. Priya Singh: For the POC we will not share raw sequences, we'll use synthetic or tokenized inputs.
[05:01] Leo Park: Good call. Now I'm going to simulate a burst. Sending 3 concurrent clients with 500 tokens each at t0.
[05:10] [05:10] System: 3 clients started
[05:20] Leo Park: Console shows the burst meter tick up — one request hit a soft cap and was routed to fallback cheaper model, one was queued, one passed through on priority lane.
[05:29] Adrian Morales: Nice, can you show the log line for the fallback?
[05:33] [05:33] Leo Park: Here, log id 7b2a — shows rule matched header X-Priority:false so it matched fallback route to model-alpha-quantized.
[05:40] Dr. Priya Singh: Question — do you support custom quantization profiles per project? Some of our models need int8 and others can be int4.
[05:49] Leo Park: Yes, model profiles can be attached at project level — Optimize suggests quantization by workload and latency targets.
[05:56] [05:56] Sophie Chen: About SLAs — what do you guarantee for Dedicated pools? We need 99.9 at least for core scoring.
[06:02] Maya Chen: Our Dedicated SLA targets are 99.9 for uptime with regional failover options. For latency SLOs we publish percentiles per model class in the model catalog; Dedicated gets reserved capacity to meet SLOs.
[06:15] Dr. Priya Singh: Any chance to run a small bench against our data so we know per-token real cost?
[06:20] Leo Park: Absolutely, that's a typical POC. We'll run your traffic sample across hosted vs dedicated variants — we'll give you latency and cost per million tokens.
[06:29] [06:29] Tomás Ruiz: For the POC, can we test both sticky routing on and off to observe KV cache warming?
[06:34] Leo Park: Yes — we'll include both scenarios in the benchmark script.
[06:38] [06:38] Rina Kapoor: Quick note: Optimize will generate batching and quantization recommendations automatically after collecting traffic stats — it can also propose autoscale settings.
[06:47] Dr. Priya Singh: On compliance, do you have an SOC2 attestation we can review?
[06:50] Maya Chen: Yes — I'll include the SOC2 Type II report. Also we have an ISO summary and our data flow docs.
[06:58] Sophie Chen: For KMS/HSM integration, is the key exchange flow documented? We need to show it to our cryptography team.
[07:03] Leo Park: We'll attach the KMS integration guide; it describes CMK provisioning steps for AWS KMS and an HSM-backed flow for on-prem.
[07:12] [07:12] Dr. Priya Singh: What's the minimal commit for Dedicated? We're a bit early stage, worried about large upfronts.
[07:18] Maya Chen: Dedicated has a couple of tiers — monthly minimums vary by region and GPU class; we can structure a short-term pilot commit for 3 months with measured scaling, or start hosted and move to Dedicated once you hit throughput thresholds.
[07:31] Adrian Morales: If we start hosted can we later import keys and traffic patterns into a Private deployment with minimal changes?
[07:36] Leo Park: Yes, the API surface is identical. We provide migration tooling to export routing policies and key maps. Some network changes are required for VPC private endpoints but the keying and quota configs are portable.
[07:50] [07:50] Maya Chen: I want to show the console policy editor. You can create a rule: if header X-Env:prod AND JWT.claims.team==scoring then route to reserved pool A with quota lane priority 100.
[08:06] [08:06] Dr. Priya Singh: That level of granularity is great. Can we also set hard token caps plus soft throttles?
[08:12] Leo Park: Yes — you can set soft caps which trigger throttling and routing, and hard caps which reject with explicit error. Soft caps are useful for graceful degradation.
[08:21] [08:21] Tomás Ruiz: How are rate limits enforced when you have multi-region replicas? We sometimes have geo-split traffic.
[08:28] Leo Park: We support regional quotas with cross-region coordination; you can also set region-specific caps in the console. When global cap is hit the system runs a reconciliation to choose which region gets priority based on policies.
[08:41] Dr. Priya Singh: We have a team in EU — need data residency. Can we scope projects to run in EU region only?
[08:47] Maya Chen: Yes, you can pin project routing and model variants to region; Private deployments can be deployed in-region for data residency requirements.
[08:55] [08:55] Adrian Morales: About monitoring — do we get request-level traces or sampling?
[08:59] Leo Park: We provide both. By default it's sampled traces plus aggregated token metrics; you can enable higher fidelity for specific keys or projects for a short window.
[09:10] Dr. Priya Singh: Good. On cost, any rules of thumb for token vs latency tradeoff with quantization?
[09:16] Rina Kapoor: Typically moving from fp16 to int8 gives 1.6-2x cost improvement; int4 can be another ~1.5x depending on model. There's a latency delta but Optimize can model both based on your request size distribution.
[09:30] [09:30] Sophie Chen: Any competitors have better locking on KMS or better VPC features? We briefly looked at MegaCloud AI — they advertised private endpoints but their quantization tooling looked weaker.
[09:40] Maya Chen: Right — Anthropic and MegaCloud AI have strengths, but Redwood focuses on the developer experience across hosting models and the cost/latency controls.
[09:50] [09:50] Leo Park: Demo pivot — I'll show the API call flow for starting a session with a project key and how the headers affect routing.
[09:58] [10:10] Leo Park: Example curl: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer proj.abc123' -H 'X-Cygnus-Pipeline:scoring' ... and you can pass sticky-session-id to pin affinity.
[10:22] Tomás Ruiz: For long jobs do you support chunked streaming and reconnect semantics?
[10:27] Leo Park: Yes, streaming with resume tokens is supported; reconnect will resume KV cache where possible if affinity is maintained.
[10:35] [10:35] Dr. Priya Singh: Can we also use the console to simulate traffic and get suggested quotas?
[10:40] Leo Park: The console has a traffic simulator, and Optimize will suggest quota settings after a short observation period.
[10:47] [10:47] Sophie Chen: How long before Optimize supplies useful recommendations? We want numbers before committing.
[10:51] Rina Kapoor: Often within 48 hours for generic batching recommendations; for deeper quantization and autoscale tips we recommend a week of traffic or the POC sample.
[11:00] [11:00] Adrian Morales: This is starting to feel actionable. For the POC, can you outline the deliverables?
[11:05] Maya Chen: POC deliverables: 1) benchmark report (latency, p50/ p95, token cost) across hosted and a reserved pool sample; 2) recommended org/project key topology and quota plan; 3) a config export you can import into Private if you go that route.
[11:20] Dr. Priya Singh: That works. Timeline? We want to start mid-August.
[11:25] Maya Chen: We can start a scoped POC the week of Aug 17 — we'll need your sample traffic and a list of high-priority pipelines.
[11:32] [11:32] Action item mention: send benchmark script
[11:36] [11:36] Leo Park: I'm going to share the benchmark repo link in the notes after the call — it's a small Python harness that replays traces and measures token throughput.
[11:45] [11:45] Sophie Chen: On legal/contracting — do you do short-term pilots with existing standard terms or do we need an enterprise addendum?
[11:51] Maya Chen: We can run a pilot under standard terms and then add an enterprise addendum for Dedicated/Private. I'll have our legal ops share the pilot contract draft.
[11:59] Dr. Priya Singh: Cool. A few quick edge questions: can you enforce redaction rules server-side for certain endpoints?
[12:04] Leo Park: Yes, server-side scrubbing rules can be applied per-project; we can redact by JSON key patterns or regex.
[12:12] [12:12] Adrian Morales: Can you programmatically adjust quotas during run (via API)? We want autoscaling triggers to increase burst lanes temporarily.
[12:18] Leo Park: You can modify quotas via API; we also expose an autoscale policy language to increase burst windows in response to observed throughput.
[12:25] [12:25] Dr. Priya Singh: Anything else we should watch out for when moving to Dedicated?
[12:30] Maya Chen: Network egress, data residency controls, and planned maintenance windows — we'll coordinate maintenance windows for Dedicated and provide a runbook.
[12:38] [12:38] Tomás Ruiz: Good to know.
[12:40] [12:40] Maya Chen: End of demo portion. Quick recap and next steps?
[12:45] Dr. Priya Singh: Please send SOC2 and KMS guide, and the benchmark script. We'll confirm POC timeline after internal planning.
[12:52] Maya Chen: Noted. I'll send pricing for a 3-month pilot and the Dedicated tiers. Leo will share benchmark assets.
[13:00] [13:00] Sophie Chen: I'll send an initial security questionnaire with questions on data retention and key lifecycle.
[13:05] Maya Chen: Perfect. Any last questions?
[13:08] Adrian Morales: No, thank you all.
[13:10] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with meeting notes and links.
[13:15] [Call ends]

References / Shared links mentioned:
- Benchmark repo: https://rwd-infra.internal/benchmarks/cygnus-poc (shared after call)
